*Job market paper · sole-authored*

**Winner of the 2026 Society for the Development of Austrian Economics Graduate Student Essay Contest.** To be presented in the contest winners session at the Southern Economic Association Annual Meeting, Houston, November 22, 2026.

[Download Paper (PDF)](../Smith_Jacob_JMP.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}

## Overview

The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 is usually remembered as one of America's first consumer-protection laws — a federal guarantee, in an age of rampant adulteration, that what the label promised was what the bottle held. This paper reads the Act through public choice instead: as a government-administered solution to a credence-goods problem the straight distillers of Kentucky and Pennsylvania could not solve privately. Their brands and marks were freely counterfeited down a distribution chain they could not police; a Treasury strip stamp, backed by federal criminal law, made their quality signal excludable in a way no private mark ever had.

The reframing yields a sharp, testable distinction. If the Act worked by **raising rivals' costs**, certified output should have grown at the expense of the rectifiers (blenders of cheaper neutral spirit) and a scarcity rent should have opened in relative prices. If it worked by **certifying quality**, a new premium tier should have grown from a near-zero base *without* the rectifying trade falling. The two mechanisms make opposite predictions — and the data can tell them apart.

The evidence comes from a **newly digitized state-by-fiscal-year panel built from the Annual Reports of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, FY1877–1920** — whiskey deposited into bond, tax-paid withdrawals, spirits rectified, distilleries operated, grain consumed, and (after 1897) withdrawals under the bottled-in-bond stamp — validated against the printed totals through 459 cross-year chain assertions and 59 zero-tolerance national control totals.

## Abstract

> "The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 created a federal strip stamp certifying single-distillery, single-season whiskey aged at least four years in bond. In 1893 a revenue official had proposed, and a House committee endorsed, a cheap stamp for every bottle, marking original packages and compounds alike. The Act confined the stamp to four-year whiskey. On newly digitized Internal Revenue accounts by state and year, rectified output rose 43 percent after the Act and did not fall relative to straight output. If the years just before the Act are a valid baseline, the design rules out a relative contraction of the rectifying trade above about 15 percent. The Act instead created a certified segment, fast-growing after 1902 amid a cultivated demand campaign and drawn in Kentucky and Pennsylvania in proportion to their stocks in bond. That fits a neutral rule too. The capture lies in the eligibility term, a four-year floor where a printed date would have answered deception. Capture can be identified by whom eligibility was written around, not only by rivals’ losses."

## A preview of the findings

**1. No foreclosure.** Foreclosure predicts that the within-state gap between straight and rectified output shifts toward straight whiskey after 1897. It did not: national rectified output averaged **43 percent more** after the Act than before, and the gap did not move toward straight whiskey. If the years just before the Act are a valid baseline, the difference-in-differences **rules out a relative contraction of the rectifying trade larger than about 15 percent**. The trade the bill's proponents complained of kept growing.

**2. A manufactured premium segment.** The genuine expansion is the certified sub-segment itself: bottled-in-bond withdrawals grew from **0.54 million gallons in 1898 to 4.79 million by 1908** — flat through FY1902, then accelerating sharply as demand was cultivated — reaching about 3 percent of straight output by 1905, a small tier expanding on top of an existing trade. Whether that volume was new or relabeled, the quantity record cannot settle: within adopting states the elasticity of non-bonded on bonded withdrawals is **−0.096 (standard error 0.108; ten states)**, and its interval covers both zero and the band that one-for-one relabeling implies. Prices are the weak record. A hedonic model of roughly two hundred hand-collected quotes puts bonded whiskey **about 10 percent** above rectified spirits, conditional on age and channel, but that gap combines the federal mark with the straight–rectified quality difference; against uncertified straight whiskey the bonded premium is about two percent, well inside its standard error. The price difference-in-differences the quotes allow is uninformative, and the price evidence is read as illustrative and bounding.

**3. Capture by eligibility.** Kentucky and Pennsylvania together took **92 percent of bonded bourbon and rye withdrawals**, roughly in proportion to the whiskey they already held in bond; Kentucky's share of bonded withdrawals equals its share of aged stocks in bond at **0.99×**. Proportional uptake fits a neutral rule too, so the capture is not in who used the stamp but in who was eligible for it. In 1893 the Deputy Commissioner of Internal Revenue proposed, and a House committee endorsed, a cheap stamp for *every* bottle that would have told buyers whether it came from a distiller's original package or was compounded. The Act kept the stamp and confined it to whiskey four years old. A printed date would have answered the deception the distillers complained of; a four-year floor wrote eligibility around the aged stock the incumbents already held. The demand for certified whiskey was then actively cultivated, with Harvey Wiley's federal purity chemists lending their authority to teach buyers to distrust uncertified spirit.

The upshot: **capture need not look like foreclosure.** A regulation can expand a market, resolve a real information asymmetry, and still be capture, identified by whom its eligibility rule was written around.

![The quantity horse-race on the FY1887–1908 one-definition panel: the event-study path (left) shows no post-Act widening of the straight–rectified gap, and rectified output (right) grew at least as fast as straight whiskey — the pattern that rejects the foreclosure reading.](../images/papers/bib_horserace.png){fig-alt="Event-study coefficients and indexed output series showing no post-Act divergence in favor of straight whiskey"}

## Key estimate

**Hedonic price model** (log price per proof gallon; rectified spirits the omitted category; channel, state, and year fixed effects):

| Variable | Coefficient | Std. error |
|---|---:|---:|
| Bottled-in-bond | +0.096 | 0.058 |
| Straight (uncertified) | +0.076 | 0.088 |
| Age (per year) | +0.074 | 0.009 |

N = 187; R² = 0.66. Standard errors clustered by source advertisement. No significance stars, following the paper: the quotes come from six states. The bonded coefficient combines the federal mark with the straight–rectified quality difference; the certification contrast (bonded minus straight) is about 0.02 log points. Illustrative and bounding; stable across real-price and high-confidence-quote specifications.
